title: Internet users engage more with phatic posts than with health misinformation on Facebook
screen_reason: Content analysis of all 500 posts published by the French Facebook page Sante + Mag over 21 days (10-31 January 2019), together with the 6,483,888 interactions they generated. Each post was manually coded as health misinformation or not by verifying every health statement on the web, checking fact-checking sites and assessing source reliability. The paper reports both the share of posts that are health misinformation (28%, 140/500) and the share of total interactions accruing to health misinformation (14.3%), giving one CONTENT and one SHARING estimate, each with a stricter 'potentially harmful' variant.

estimates.measure_type: % of the Facebook page's posts classified as health misinformation
estimates.denominator: 500 posts, all posts published by the Facebook page Sante + Mag between 10 and 31 January 2019
estimates.definition: Post classified as health misinformation after verifying the validity of each health-related statement by web research, checking whether the content had been debunked by a fact-checking website, and assessing the reliability of any scientific source mentioned
estimates.misinfo_def: "health misinformation" to refer to information "that is contrary to the epistemic consensus of the scientific community regarding a phenomenon" (Swire-Thompson and Lazer, 2019, p. 14.2)
estimates.source_quote: Out of 500 posts analyzed, 28% (140/500) fit in the category
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'What types of content are published by Sante + Mag?', p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: All 500 posts coded manually by the first author; the second author plus three independent coders blind to the hypotheses each coded 50 randomly selected posts. Cohen's kappa agreement with the first author ranged from 85.55% to 90.91% ('substantial' for two coders, 'almost perfect' for two).
estimates.moderator_quote: These volumes represent all the posts published by Sante + Mag, and all the interactions they generated, over a period of 21 days from January 10 to January 31, 2019.
estimates.notes: Full census of one page's output over the window, hence sampling_frame=full_census and denom_selection=single_source. denom_scope coded topical: Sante + Mag is a health page, though a large share of its posts are non-health gossip and phatic content.

estimates.notes: Coded SHARING (sharing_subtype content_share) because the denominator is engagement, not items that exist. Interactions pool reactions, comments and shares, so this is an engagement share rather than a pure reshare share. unit='exposure' is the nearest schema value for an engagement event; no 'interaction' value exists.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the complements 85.8% of interactions from non-health-misinformation and 89.3% from content unlikely to cause harm - exact complements of the extracted values, and R8 forbids keeping computed complements; both happen to be stated verbatim but add nothing. (b) 79.3% of health misinformation posts contained at least one cognitive factor of attraction - computed inside the misinformation-only subsample, but it measures attention-grabbing features, not falsity, so R3's within_misinfo_content case does not apply and no row was made. (c) Cognitive-factor prevalences among all posts (social relations 50.4%, threat 27.8%, sexuality 14.0%, disgust 2.6%, any factor 82.0%) and social sub-topic shares (family 34.9%, love 31.8%) are content-feature codings, not misinformation. (d) The exploratory comment analysis of the five most-commented harmful-misinformation posts (3% approval, 12% criticism, 48% jokes or social purposes, out of 4737 comments) is a share of comments computed inside a misinformation-only set and describes audience reaction, not misinformation prevalence. (e) Post-format shares (66.6% articles, 24.0% photos, 9.4% videos) are format descriptors. (f) The regression coefficients and the 66.09%/55% of interactions catalyzed by phatic and positive posts concern other content categories, not misinformation.

rob.design: Observational content analysis of real-world platform data. Frame: complete census of the 500 posts published by the Facebook page Sante + Mag between 10 and 31 January 2019, with all 6,483,888 interactions retrieved via the CrowdTangle API. Representativeness argued by comparing post-format proportions in the window to the page's 12-month averages. Coding: every post coded by the first author against a written category scheme (health misinformation; potentially harmful; emotional valence; five cognitive factors of attraction; eight social sub-topics; phatic or not). Reliability: four additional coders (the second author plus three blind to the hypotheses) each coded 50 randomly selected posts; Cohen's kappa agreement with the first author 85.55-90.91%. Single page, single country, 21-day window; no sampling weights or response rate apply.
rob.item6_quote: The first step to code our sample was to evaluate how many posts could be classified as health misinformation. We did so by verifying the validity of each health-related statement by conducting research on the web; by checking if their content had been debunked by a fact-checking website; and by assessing the reliability of each scientific source mentioned.
rob.item10_quote: Out of 500 posts analyzed, 28% (140/500) fit in the category health misinformation, and 21% (105/500) were assessed as potentially harmful.
